unit.can_do_en: start and end a phone call and leave a message.

judge.reason: Moi/Hei greeting, sä/sinä, mulle/minulle are only register differences.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Joo! Mä jätin viestin. Kuulitsä sen?
lines.text_kirja: Kyllä! Minä jätin viestin. Kuulitko sinä sen?
lines.gloss_en: Yes! I left a message. Did you hear it?

judge.reason: Joo/Kyllä, mä/minä, and 'Kuulit sä' vs 'Kuulitko sinä' are the same question and meaning.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_kirja: Voitko sinä hakea minut asemalta huomenna?
lines.gloss_en: Can you pick me up from the station tomorrow?

judge.reason: Both ask whether you can pick me up from the station tomorrow; hakee/hakea and mut/minut are register differences.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.text_puhe: Totta kai. Mihin aikaan juna tulee?
lines.text_kirja: Totta kai. Mihin aikaan juna tulee?
lines.gloss_en: Of course. What time does the train arrive?

judge.reason: Puol is spoken for puoli; both mean half past three.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.text_puhe: Okei, mä oon siel. Laita viesti, jos juna on myöhäs.
lines.text_kirja: Selvä, minä olen siellä. Lähetä viesti, jos juna on myöhässä.
lines.gloss_en: OK, I'll be there. Send a message if the train is late.

judge.reason: Okei/Selvä, siel/siellä, myöhäs/myöhässä are register differences; 'laita viesti' and 'lähetä viesti' both mean send a message.
Moikka and Kuulemiin are both goodbyes, and the rest is the same.

forms.why_en: Moi is the everyday spoken hello. Books and formal texts write hei.
Means 'you' (one person). Spoken: 'sä'.
Adds -i for the past and -t for 'you': soittaa becomes soitit, tt turning to t.
Minä with -lle for 'for'. Speech shortens it to mulle.
Yes. In everyday speech people often say joo instead.
Means 'I'. Spoken Finnish often says 'mä'.
Adds -i for the past and -n for 'I': jättää becomes jätin, tt turning to t.
Viesti, message. The thing you send takes -n here: viestin, a whole message.

forms.form_name_en: past tense, 2nd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Adds -i for the past, -t for 'you' and -ko to ask: kuulitko. Speech drops -ko: kuulit sä.
Se with -n when the whole thing is the object: kirjoittaa sen.
Ei with -n for 'I': en, I do not.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
The partitive of mikä, what. Mitä saa olla? means What can I get you?
The partitive singular of asia 'matter': 'Mitä asiaa?' means 'What's it about?'

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 2nd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Voit with -ko asks 'can you?': voitko. Speech drops -ko and adds sä: voitsä.

forms.lemma_meaning_en: to fetch, to pick up, to apply
forms.why_en: Speech turns the ea at the end into ee: hakea becomes hakee. Books write hakea.
The accusative singular of minä: minut, 'me' as the one picked up. Speech says mut.
Adds -lta for 'from': asema becomes asemalta.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
From tosi, true. Totta kai means of course.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Mikä with -hin for 'to': mihin, where to.
Aika with -an. Mihin aikaan? means at what time?
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Tulla, to come, in the form for he, she or it: tulee.
Puoli neljä means 'half to four', so 3.30. Speech drops the last i: puol.
'Four.' The number stays in nominative singular; the counted word after it changes form.
Okei is the everyday spoken OK. Books write selvä, which means clear.
Means 'am': present tense, 1st person singular, so it goes with 'minä'. Spoken: 'oon'.
Siellä means there. Speech shortens -llä to -l: Siellä becomes Siel.
Lähettää, to send. To tell one person to do it, drop the ending: lähetä. Speech often says laita, 'put', instead.

Means 'is': present tense, 3rd person singular, going with 'Helsinki'.
Myöhässä means 'late, behind time'. Speech shortens -ssä to -s: Myöhässä becomes Myöhäs.
Tehdä 'to do' becomes tee- and adds -n for 'I': teen. People say it the same way.

Kuulemiin is the polite goodbye on the phone. In everyday speech people say moikka instead.
